On January 2, his personally led litter-bearer squads into a fiercely contested area of the Ipo Dam Hills, while serving with the First Battalion, First Infantry Regiment.

His infantry unit had suffered many casualties. Despite withering enemy rifle, machinegun, and mortar fire, he gave medical aid to the wounded men and directed their evacuation to the battalion aid station.

With utter disregard for his own safety, he administered blood plasma to the more seriously wounded, and personally carried them to the shelter of a nearby crater.

Makes Dangerous Trips

When medical supplies were about to run short, he replenished them by making several difficult and dangerous trips, unescorted, to the aid station.

For his actions, the Phoenician was awarded the first Silver Star. The battle continued unabated throughout the day and into the night, accompanied by his motorcycle and the ground. Heavily-Decorated Hero Returns Home

By PEG MAGIE

ONE OF Phoenix's most highly decorated heroes, First Lt. Marshall D. Savoy, is home on convalescent leave.

An assistant battalion surgeon, Lieutenant Savoy was honored for repeatedly risking his life to aid wounded comrades. The veteran's forgetfulness of self and gallantry under fire twice earned him the Silver Star, while serving in the Pacific theater.

In addition to the high combat award, the lieutenant holds the Soldier's Medal, which military men count even harder to win than the Silver Star. The Soldier's Medal is awarded for "heroism not involving actual combat with the enemy." It was presented to Lieutenant Savoy three days after Japan surrendered.

His other decorations include the Purple Heart with cluster, the Asiatic-Pacific ribbon with two battle stars, a bronze arrowhead for an amphibious landing; Combat Medic Badge; Philippine Liberation ribbon; American Theater ribbon; Victory ribbon, and a unit citation.

A native of the Salt River valley, Savoy joined the regular army as a private in January 1940. After 21 months overseas, he is here now with his wife, Rebecca, and three-year-old son, Teddy, at his home on Southern avenue near 27th street.
